en: Theravāda Vinaya Bhikkhunīvibhaṅga Pācittiyakaṇḍa
The Chapter on Turning Back, 34.
The Training Rule on Not Attending to One’s Needs.
At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
Now at that time, the bhikkhunī Thullanandā neither attended to her afflicted co-resident nor made any effort to have her attended to.
Those bhikkhunīs who were of few desires... [being] indignant, critical, and complaining, said:
"How can the noble lady Thullanandā neither attend to her afflicted co-resident nor make any effort to have her attended to?"... [as before]...

“Is it true, monks, that the nun Thullanandā neither attends to her afflicted co-resident nor makes an effort to have her attended to? “It is true, Blessed One. The Buddha, the Blessed One, rebuked her... [as before] ...“How can this foolish woman, monks, neither attend to her afflicted co-resident nor make an effort to have her attended to? This will not lead to the benefit of many people... [as before] ...“And so, monks, this training rule should be recited thus: ‘If a nun, knowing that a co-resident is afflicted, neither attends to her nor makes an effort to have her attended to, she commits an offense of wrong-doing.’”

"How indeed, monks, could the bhikkhunī Thullanandā neither attend to her afflicted co-resident nor make an effort to have her attended to? This, monks, is neither for the inspiration of those without faith... And thus, monks, should the bhikkhunīs recite this training rule: "Whatever bhikkhunī, when her co-resident is afflicted, does not herself attend to her or make an effort to have her attended to, that bhikkhunī is to be admonished by the bhikkhunīs thus: ‘Sister, when your co-resident is afflicted, you should either attend to her yourself or make an effort to have her attended to.

If, being thus admonished by the bhikkhunīs, she should say: ‘I will not attend to her, nor will I make an effort to have her attended to; what is that to you? that bhikkhunī is to be admonished two or three times by the bhikkhunīs for the sake of relinquishing that course of action. If, being admonished two or three times, she relinquishes it, that is good. If she does not relinquish it, that bhikkhunī is also subject to expulsion (pārājikā) and is no longer in communion."
“Whatever nun, however, does not attend to a co-resident sister who is suffering, nor makes an effort to have her attended to, commits an offense entailing confession (pācittiya).
Regarding “whatever nun”: whoever she may be... [and so forth].
"Bhikkhunī" ...
[as before] ... this is the kind of bhikkhunī intended in this context.
"Afflicted" means:
"Ill" refers to one who is sick.
"Co-resident" refers to a student living with her preceptor.
"He should not attend to them" means he should not attend to them himself.
"He should not make an effort to have them attended to" means...
She should not command another.
If she merely lays down the burden, thinking, "I will neither attend nor make an effort to have someone else attend," there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
If she neither attends to her own female pupil nor to one who is not fully ordained, nor makes an effort to have them attended to, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
There is no offense if there is an obstacle,
or if one does not obtain it after having searched for it.
For one who is ill,
in cases of emergency,
for one who is insane,
"For one who is a first offender":
thus ends the fourth training rule.
